title: How Recursive Functions Work
concept: When a function calls itself, a new stack frame is pushed each time

steps.title: Including header file
steps.explanation:
We include the standard I/O library with **`#include <stdio.h>`** to use `printf`.

The topic of this lesson is the **recursive function** -- a structure where a function calls itself.

steps.title: Starting main function
steps.explanation:
**`int main()`** -- The entry point of the program. A dedicated **stack frame** for main is created.

The `countdown` function defined above has not been called yet, so it has not executed.

steps.title: Calling countdown(3) - first recursive frame
steps.explanation: **`countdown(3);`** -- A **new stack frame** for `countdown` is pushed on top of main, and the parameter `n` receives a copy of `3`. main is paused here and waits until countdown(3) finishes.

steps.title: n=3: Check termination condition and print
steps.explanation: Upon entering countdown, it first checks `if (n <= 0)`. Since `3 <= 0` is false, the if block is skipped, and **`printf("%d...\n", n)`** prints `"3..."`.

steps.title: Calling countdown(2) - second recursive frame
steps.explanation: **`countdown(n - 1);`** -- Inside `countdown(3)`, `countdown(2)` is called. Another new stack frame is pushed on top, so now there are **3 frames** in total: main (waiting) -> countdown(n=3, waiting) -> countdown(n=2, active).

steps.title: Calling countdown(1) - third recursive frame
steps.explanation: In countdown(2), `n <= 0` is also false -> prints `"2..."` -> calls **`countdown(1)`**, repeating the same process. The stack has now grown to **4 layers**. Looking at `n` in each frame: layer 2 `n=3`(0x1004), layer 3 `n=2`(0x1008), layer 4 `n=1`(0x100c) -- each has its own independent copy.

steps.title: countdown(0) - base case reached!
steps.explanation: After countdown(1) prints `"1..."`, it calls `countdown(0)`. This time `0 <= 0` is **true** -- the **base case** has finally been reached!

steps.title: Stack frame unwinding
steps.explanation: As countdown(0) returns, its frame is **popped**, and the waiting countdown(1) resumes. Since there is no remaining code, countdown(1) also returns, and in the same way countdown(2) -> countdown(3) -> main return in order.

quiz.question: When countdown(3) is executed, what is the maximum number of countdown frames that exist on the stack simultaneously?
quiz.explanation:
countdown(3) -> countdown(2) -> countdown(1) -> countdown(0) results in a total of 4 calls.
When countdown(0) reaches the base case, 4 countdown frames exist on the stack simultaneously.

misconceptions.wrong: Recursive calls reuse the same stack frame since it's the same function
misconceptions.correct: A completely new stack frame is created for every call.
misconceptions.why: Even though it's the same function, separate memory space (a frame) is allocated for each call, so the n variable in each frame holds an independent value.

misconceptions.wrong: Recursion stops on its own without a base case
misconceptions.correct: Without a base case, calls continue infinitely and a Stack Overflow occurs.
misconceptions.why: Stack memory is finite (usually 1-8MB), so continuously pushing frames without a base case will exhaust the memory.

keyTakeaway: A recursive function pushes a new stack frame with each call, and when the base case is reached, the frames unwind in reverse order.
